newsitem.title: USA: Aetna cost cuts critical to merger success.
newsitem.headline: Aetna cost cuts critical to merger success.

text.p: Aetna Inc took a critical step toward making its merger with U.S. Healthcare succeed on Thursday when it announced a restructuring and a major round of layoffs, analysts said.
"This is a necessary move," said Mark Puccia, director of insurance rating services at Standard & Poor's. "It was absolutely critical that they take this move to make the combination work," he said.
Aetna agreed to buy U.S. Healthcare in April in a $8.9 billion cash and stock transaction.

"Any time you have an organization that pays close to $9 billion for a company that others wouldn't have paid nearly as much for, it's natural that they're going to look for substantial cost reductions to justify the transaction," Puccia said.
Aetna said it will consolidate its 40 customer service centers into six regional service centers supported by a few additional secondary sites.
The healthcare restructuring will result in the elimination of about 7,500 jobs by the end of 1998.
But the addition of new jobs will bring the net job loss to about 4,000 in the healthcare business.
Before the merger, Aetna said it had about 23,000 employees in its healthcare busness and U.S. Healthcare had about 5,000.
Aetna said it has a total of about 33,700 employees.
Most of the layoffs will come from the ranks of Aetna employees, an Aetna spokeswoman said.
"The large majority will be from Aetna," she said, noting that Aetna had five times as many employees and that Aetna have 40 service centers while U.S. Healthcare had only three.
Most of the layoffs are related to the service center closings, she said.
Aetna also said it will eliminate 700 jobs in its retirement services business, but said the net reduction will come to only about 400 after accounting for the creation of additional new jobs.
Aetna declined to project the cost savings from the restructuring, but said they are in line with its previously-announced target of $140 million of after-tax administrative cost savings.
Aetna said it does not expect to take any more major cost-cutting steps in the near future.
"We do not currently foresee any restructuring actions in the foreseeable future," the Aetna spokeswoman said.
Despite the magnitude of the layoffs, Standard & Poor's Puccia said he was not concerned that Aetna had gone too far.
"We don't think they're cutting out muscle along with the fat," he said. "This is a level they can support."
Although Aetna was expected to cut jobs to eliminate duplication, it also was expected to cut other jobs as part of a strategic retooling of the two companies, analysts said.

"It goes beyond just eliminating the duplication," one source familiar with the situation said. Instead, there will be some operational restructuring as well as Aetna attempts to create a new company out of the two previous ones.
"It's really a combination of the two, not just making Aetna look like U.S. Healthcare," he said.
But adapting to U.S. Healthcare's way of doing business will be a part of the restructuring, Puccia said.
Part of the cost cuts, he said, are expected to come as Aetna negotiates new, more favorable contracts with its healthcare providers comparable to those at U.S. Healthcare.
"They are aggressively going out and recontracting with their providers," Puccia said.
In addition, Aetna hopes to generate new revenue by selling its traditional non-medical products, such as group life, dental and disability insurance, to the former U.S. Healthcare customers.
Aetna also must expand beyond into new markets if its integration plans are to succeed, analysts said.

"What they have to do is show the world that they can integrate U.S. Healthcare and Aetna," said Todd Richter, an analyst with Dean Witter. "They have to show the world that, now that they've gone through this long process, they picked the right people."
"U.S. Healthcare has a lot of strength in the Northeast," he said. "Now they also have to show people that they can export U.S. Healthcare expertise outside of the Northeast."
Aetna shares fell 1-3/8 to 66-1/2 in late trading.
